catalog_citation: Onyango, Jacktone Okello. 2006. Verb tonology in Olunyala. PhD thesis, Kenyatta University, Nairobi. Kenyatta University Institutional Repository, handle 123456789/2009 (https://ir-library.ku.ac.ke/handle/123456789/2009;scan, 186 pp; repository text).
catalog_locator: Chapter 2, §2.2.4 Lexical Phonology and Morphology, principle (vi) 'The Principle of Underspecification', pp. 42-43 (the sentence breaks at the page boundary: p. 42 ends 'because', p. 43 begins 'it invariably'); tone statement p. 2 (§1.2).
catalog_quote: (vi) The Principle of Underspecification. The primary objective of this principle is to enable us to write the most economical grammar possible. Essentially, this principle eliminates redundant features in the rule specification. For example, stress is not specified in Olunyala grammar because [p. 42 | p. 43] it invariably falls on the penultimate syllable. Similarly, only high (H) tones are specified in the underlying representation but low (L) tones are not. This is because the H tone is the marked feature whereas the L tone is the unmarked feature that is filled in by default rule. [pp. 42-43] ... Olunyala is a tone language, like most Bantu languages. [p. 2]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Olunyala (Busia) is a two-tone (H/L) register tone language ('Olunyala is a tone language, like most Bantu languages', p. 2); the author, a native speaker, states that stress is fully predictable and therefore left unspecified in the grammar: it always falls on the penultimate syllable of the word.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the source says stress 'invariably' falls on the penult. No mention of interaction with contrastive vowel length or with phrase position.
new_statements.domain_note: The remark is incidental, made while illustrating the underspecification principle of Lexical Phonology in a theory chapter; the thesis itself is about verb tone (H/L, 'right-edge tone language'), and stress is not otherwise analysed or measured. Domain is the word (grammar-level statement); no distinction is drawn between citation forms and phrase-internal words.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog west2861 "West Nyala" is the Lunyala of Bunyala (lake-shore Busia County, Port Victoria), distinct from East Nyala [nle, east2409] of Kakamega/Navakholo; the two are not mutually intelligible (Glottolog note citing Kanyoro 1983 and Ochwaya-Oluoch 2003:7-8). The quoted source, Onyango 2006, states (p. 8 and p. 24 fn. 1) that it is "restricted to the Olunyala language spoken in Busia district", i.e. west2861, and explicitly separates it from the Abanyala of Kakamega. Marlo's 2007 dissertation "Lunyala(-West)" is the same Busia variety. Etakwa's KU thesis on "Olunyala (K)" and (per Glottolog's tagging) Ochwaya-Oluoch 2003 concern the Kakamega variety [nle] and were not used.

tone_statements.citation: Marlo, Michael R. 2013. Verb tone in Bantu languages: micro-typological patterns and research methods. Africana Linguistica 19: 137-234. doi:10.3406/aflin.2013.1020
tone_statements.quote: (21) Bantu languages with predictable verbal tonal systems a. varieties of southwestern Luyia including Khayo (Marlo 2009a), one variety of Marachi (Bruckhaus 2012), Nyala-West (Marlo 2007, Onyango 2006), Saamia (Poletto 1998a), and Tura (Marlo 2008b) [p.154] ... In predictable and reversive languages that are marked with an inflectional H in all verb forms, we expect that the causative and/ or passive would have widespread tonal effects within the tone system, as it does in the predictable language Nyala-West (Marlo 2007). [p.182]
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Predictable Luyia system: verb roots toneless, grammatical (melodic) H tones assigned by TAM/clause type in every verb form; H-toned object prefixes/reflexive, causative-passive H, and enclitic Hs interact with the melodies.

tone_statements.citation: Ebarb, Kristopher & Michael R. Marlo. 2010. Conditioning factors in the realization of tone: LuNyala verbs. IULC Working Papers (Indiana University Linguistics Club Working Papers Online) 10(2) [African Linguistics Across the Discipline]. ISSN 1524-2110.
tone_statements.quote: Nyala-West (Bantu, Kenya) marks tense-aspect-mood-polarity and clause-type distinctions in verbs with grammatical H tones, called melodic Hs. Nyala-West has six basic tonal melodies in which melodic Hs target three positions of the verbal stem: the first mora of the stem, the first mora of the second syllable of the stem, and the final mora of the stem. The present paper shows how certain aspects of the prosody of the verb stem, the presence or absence of H-toned affixes, and the application of several tonal processes influence the realization of the melodic H in two of the tonal melodies of Nyala-West.
tone_statements.locator: Abstract, OJS article landing page (DC.Description meta), IULCWP 10(2) article 25986
tone_statements.summary: Privative /H/ vs zero system with grammatical 'melodic H' tones: 6 verbal tone melodies docking to 3 stem positions (mora-based TBU); realization conditioned by stem prosody, H-toned prefixes and tone rules.
